name: Collection, staging and exfiltration
description: Detections for the last stage: gathering data, compressing it somewhere writable, and pushing it out. Individually these are the weakest rules in the pack, because archiving a file and uploading a file are ordinary work. They earn their score by stacking on top of a credential-access or LOLBin hit in the same process, which is what the correlating engine in DetectionEngine is for.

rules.title: Archive created in a staging directory
rules.description: Collected data is almost always compressed before it leaves, and it is compressed somewhere the current user can write without prompting. On its own this is background noise; immediately after a credential-store read it is the middle of an exfiltration chain.
rules.author: ProcessShield
falsePositives: Installers, updaters and browsers unpack and produce archives in temp directories constantly. Any build system does the same. This rule is designed to contribute to a score, not to alert alone.

rules.title: Archive utility invoked with a password switch
rules.description: A password on the archive stops content inspection at the proxy and at the DLP gateway. Legitimate users do password-protect archives, but doing it from a script, into a temp directory, is a different thing from a person zipping a document.
rules.author: ProcessShield
falsePositives: Backup scripts legitimately encrypt their output, and some vendors ship password-protected support bundles.
The pattern requires the password to be on the command line; an interactive prompt or a response file will not be seen at all.

rules.title: Archive utility pointed at a user data directory
rules.description: Compressing Documents, Desktop or a browser profile directory wholesale is collection, not housekeeping. The interesting part is the source path, not the tool.
rules.author: ProcessShield
falsePositives: Users and backup scripts archive their own Documents and Desktop folders legitimately, and developers tar source trees under their profile.

rules.title: PowerShell compressing data in-process
rules.description: Compress-Archive and the .NET ZipFile class avoid dropping an archiving utility on disk, so a detection that only watches 7z.exe and rar.exe misses them entirely. This rule covers the scripted path.
rules.author: ProcessShield
falsePositives: Log-collection, reporting and deployment scripts use Compress-Archive routinely; it is the idiomatic way to zip something in PowerShell.

rules.title: Contact with an anonymous file-upload service
rules.description: Anonymous upload services need no account, return a share link immediately and are reachable over ordinary HTTPS, which makes them the path of least resistance for pushing a staged archive off the endpoint.
rules.author: ProcessShield
falsePositives: Users share large files through these services when email attachment limits get in the way, and support engineers use transfer.sh for log bundles.
The list is a snapshot: these services appear and disappear monthly, so a miss proves nothing.

rules.title: Script host uploading to consumer cloud storage
rules.description: Consumer cloud storage is allowed almost everywhere and carries a reputable TLS certificate, so exfiltration through it survives both domain blocking and casual inspection. A script host, rather than the vendor's own sync client, is what makes this suspicious.
rules.author: ProcessShield
falsePositives: Automation and reporting scripts legitimately call graph.microsoft.com and googleapis.com; in a Microsoft 365 estate that endpoint in particular is used by a great deal of sanctioned tooling. Consider removing it and keeping only the consumer-storage hosts.

rules.title: Bulk sync utility copying to a remote target
rules.description: rclone is the standard tool in ransomware double-extortion for moving hundreds of gigabytes to cloud storage in one command. It is also a completely legitimate backup tool, so the presence of a remote target in the command line is what carries the signal.
rules.author: ProcessShield
falsePositives: rclone and WinSCP are ordinary administrator tools; scheduled backups to cloud storage look identical to exfiltration at the command-line layer. Whether the destination is a sanctioned bucket is the deciding factor and this rule cannot see it.

rules.title: Command line performing an HTTP upload of a file
rules.description: A multipart form post or a binary body from curl or PowerShell, referencing a file on disk, is an upload. Combined with an archive created moments earlier in the same process, it closes the collect-stage-exfiltrate chain.
rules.author: ProcessShield
falsePositives: CI pipelines, crash-report uploaders and vendor telemetry agents all POST files. On a build server this rule is not usable as written.

rules.title: Script host connecting to an FTP port
rules.description: FTP is unauthenticated-by-default in practice, unencrypted, and rarely inspected as carefully as HTTP. A script host opening a control connection to port 21 is either a decade-old integration or someone moving data out.
rules.author: ProcessShield
falsePositives: Legacy line-of-business integrations still push files to external FTP servers on a schedule; those are usually a short, stable list worth allowlisting by address.

rules.title: Script host connecting directly to an SMTP port
rules.description: Mailing data out from a script bypasses the mail client, the DLP hook attached to it and often the outbound proxy. Excluding the real mail clients leaves the cases worth reading.
rules.author: ProcessShield
falsePositives: Send-MailMessage in a monitoring or backup script is an extremely common way to report job status, and it will fire this rule on every run. Baseline those scripts before enabling in a production estate.

rules.title: DNS query whose leading label is a long hex chunk
rules.description: Encoding data as hex in the leftmost label is the simplest DNS exfiltration scheme there is, and it is visible because a legitimate hostname is essentially never 32 or more hex characters with nothing else in it.
rules.author: ProcessShield
falsePositives: Several antivirus and anti-spam products encode reputation lookups as hex labels; the exclusion list names the ones this pack knows about and will need extending for your stack.

rules.title: WebDAV UNC path used in a command line
rules.description: The \\host@SSL\path form makes Windows mount a remote WebDAV share as if it were a file server, so a plain copy command becomes an upload over HTTPS to an arbitrary internet host. Firewall rules that watch SMB do not see it.
rules.author: ProcessShield
falsePositives: Some organisations legitimately map SharePoint or a WebDAV document store this way, particularly on older estates that predate the sync client.

rules.title: Script capturing the screen or the clipboard
rules.description: CopyFromScreen and Get-Clipboard are the two cheapest collection primitives in PowerShell: no P/Invoke, no dropped tool, and both are frequently the first thing a stealer script does after establishing itself.
rules.author: ProcessShield
falsePositives: Screenshot utilities, clipboard managers and helpdesk diagnostic scripts use these APIs for their stated purpose.

rules.title: Office document or PDF written into a staging directory
rules.description: Documents appearing one after another in Temp, ProgramData or Users\Public is what automated collection looks like before the archive step. A single file is meaningless; the engine's per-process scoring is what turns a stream of them into a signal.
rules.author: ProcessShield
falsePositives: Office autosave, print spooling and PDF printing all write documents to temp paths; the exclusion list covers the obvious producers but not every viewer or converter installed on a machine.
Email clients other than Outlook write attachments to temp when the user opens them.
